I am 74 years old this year, and I have been farming these fields in Quzhou since I was a young boy. I never went to school, but I know this land better than anyone. My bones ache in the winter now, and I cannot lift what I used to, but my youngest son still lives nearby and brings his tractor when I need heavy work done. I have four mu of good flat land by the village.

The winter wheat went into the ground last October, just like it always does. I sowed the same improved variety I have been using for years—the seed dealer in town sells it, and it does well here. Now that spring has come and the wheat is waking up, I will topdress it with fertilizer and irrigate it three more times before harvest in early June. I always put down plenty of nitrogen because I have seen what happens when you skimp—the yield drops. After I cut the wheat, I will plant maize the same day or the next. There is no time to waste between crops. For the maize, I buy hybrid seed from the dealer; it costs more, but the yield is much better. I will not till the soil for the maize—I will plant directly into the wheat stubble to save time and diesel. The maize only needs watering twice, and I will spray for pests and weeds a few times on both crops.

I do not grow cotton or vegetables on the big field anymore. At my age, I cannot manage the extra labor, and the wheat-maize rotation feeds my family and brings in enough cash. My wife and I eat some of the grain, and the rest I sell. This is the way my father did it, and this is what I will do.
